prompt.context: Your client is a local municipality in California. The town recently built a complex of six parking lots, encircling a nearby community center and outdoor mall, which features shopping, restaurants, and some light attractions. In total there are 20,000 parking spots in these lots.
prompt.question: Our client wants to maximize the profit it generates from the parking lots, with a focus on revenue. Help our client think through the issue — how could you think about different types of pricing structures and revenue models for the parking lots?

exhibits.title: California Parking Lot — Current Rate and Occupancy Data
exhibits.shows: A table with two customer segments (Tourists/Shoppers and Store Owners), showing the parking rate and current occupancy breakdown for each segment.

tourists_shoppers.breakdown: 75% park for less than 5 hours (average 3 hours); 25% park for 5 hours or more

framework: Evaluate pricing structures: daily/hourly rates vs. monthly passes
Consider service tiers: valet vs. self-parking
Explore validation model: stores pay to validate parking for purchasing customers
Analyze tiered pricing by location: higher prices for spots closer to stores, lower for distant spots
Assess revenue from third parties beyond direct parkers (sponsors, events, advertisers)
Conduct pros/cons or cost-revenue analysis for each option to identify optimal mix

questions.prompt: Walk through Exhibit 1, then calculate the total daily revenue the parking lots currently generate.
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify two revenue streams (tourist/shopper hourly revenue and store owner permit revenue) and calculate each separately before summing. Strong candidates will note the $10 cap creates two sub-segments among tourists. Should arrive at $50,000 total daily revenue.

math.setup: 20,000 total spots. Tourist/Shopper occupancy = 30% × 20,000 = 6,000 spots. Store Owner permits = 5% × 20,000 = 1,000 permits. Tourist sub-segment A: 75% × 6,000 = 4,500 spots, avg 3 hrs at $2/hr. Tourist sub-segment B: 25% × 6,000 = 1,500 spots, 5+ hrs capped at $10 max.
steps: Sub-segment A daily revenue: 4,500 spots × 3 hrs × $2/hr = $27,000
Store owner daily revenue: 1,000 permits × $240/month ÷ 30 days = $8,000

questions.prompt: Is there a way to generate revenue from someone other than the people actually parking their cars? If we move to a store validation model — where a store validates the ticket of any customer who buys an item — spots taken increase to 10,000, the cost per validation is $5 charged to the store, and every person parking purchases an item. The number of monthly permits drops to 750. What is the impact on daily revenue?
questions.guidance: Candidate should first brainstorm third-party revenue sources (ads, sponsorships, store fees), then pivot to the quantitative validation model. Key insight: tourist/shopper revenue switches from hourly to a flat $5 per validated spot; permit revenue drops. Net change is +$6,000/day.

math.setup: Validation model: 10,000 spots validated at $5 per spot (store pays). Permits: 750 × $240/month ÷ 30 days.
steps: New tourist/shopper revenue: 10,000 spots × $5 = $50,000 (was $42,000, increase of $8,000)
New store owner revenue: 750 permits × $240 ÷ 30 = $6,000 (was $8,000, decrease of $2,000)

questions.prompt: Do you see any risks to a validation pricing model? Do you think you are likely to run into any resistance? From which types of stores and why?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates distinguish store economics: high-margin / high-ticket stores (e.g., Tiffany & Co.) can easily absorb a flat $5 fee. Low-margin / low-ticket stores (e.g., an ice cream shop) could see the $5 fee exceed their profit per transaction, making every validated sale unprofitable. Resistance will come from stores with low profit dollars per transaction.

questions.prompt: How else could you structure a validation model in order to get less pushback from store owners?
questions.guidance: Instead of a flat $5 fee per validation, charge a percentage of the transaction value or a percentage of profit per transaction. This aligns the parking cost with the store's ability to pay and removes the risk for low-margin stores.

questions.prompt: How else could we monetize the excess parking spaces beyond the standard parking and validation models?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm creatively across multiple categories: events (concerts, street fairs, farmers markets), sports (roller hockey rinks, overflow parking for large sporting events like the U.S. Open), transportation (commuter park-and-ride with bus pickup), and commercial use (food trucks, pop-up markets).

brainstorming.prompt: Brainstorm as many different pricing structures and revenue models as possible for the 20,000-spot parking complex.

categories.name: Direct Parking Revenue Models
ideas: Hourly rate with daily maximum cap
Monthly permit / pass system
Weekly or annual passes
Dynamic/surge pricing during peak hours or events
Premium pricing for covered or closer spots
Discounted off-peak rates to drive utilization

categories.name: Service Tier Differentiation
ideas: Valet parking at premium rate
Reserved spot guarantee for a fee
EV charging spots at premium
Handicap and family-priority spots

categories.name: Third-Party / Indirect Revenue
ideas: Store validation model (stores pay per validated ticket)
Advertising on ticket receipts, signage, and lot infrastructure
Sponsorship naming rights for individual lots
Revenue share with food trucks or pop-up vendors in unused areas

categories.name: Event and Alternate Use
ideas: Rent lots for concerts, festivals, street fairs
Seasonal events (holiday markets, roller rinks)
Overflow parking for nearby stadiums or arenas
Commuter park-and-ride with transit connections

categories.name: Technology and Data
ideas: Mobile app with pre-booking and guaranteed spot
License plate recognition for faster entry/exit
Loyalty rewards program to encourage repeat visits
Sell anonymized traffic/footfall data to retailers

recommendation: Move to a validation model for the parking lot to increase both utilization and daily revenue
Negotiate validation terms with store owners, ensuring the fee structure reflects store economics
risks: Pushback from low-margin stores whose profit per transaction is less than the validation fee
Risk of lower permit revenue as fewer store owners take monthly passes under the new model
Potential underutilization if validation uptake by stores is low
next_steps: Run analysis to determine optimal validation fee structure (flat fee vs. percentage of transaction vs. percentage of profit) by store category
Negotiate pilot agreements with a subset of stores before full rollout
Explore additional monetization of unused capacity through events and commuter programs
